reason: Barnard's Star offers a compelling narrative about the sky's fastest-moving star, disproven exoplanet claims, and interstellar travel concepts, fully supported by 16 multi-sourced claims.
story: In 1916, astronomer Edward Emerson Barnard made a stunning discovery in the constellation Ophiuchus: a dim red dwarf star sprinting across the sky faster than any other known star. Located just six light-years away, Barnard's Star travels 10.3 arcseconds per year, covering a distance equal to the full Moon's diameter every 180 years. Hurtling toward us at over 100 kilometers per second, it will make its closest approach around 11,800 CE at under four light-years away. Yet despite its extreme proximity and ancient age—nearly twice as old as our Sun—it is so faint at magnitude 9.5 that you need a telescope to see it. Its cosmic motion and close range made it the primary target for Project Daedalus, humanity's 1970s theoretical interstellar starship study. For decades, astronomers debated claims of planets around it, with famous false alarms eventually disproven by stellar activity.
angle: Barnard's Star moves across our night sky faster than any other known star—crossing a full Moon's width every 180 years—yet despite being our second-closest star system, it is completely invisible to the naked eye.

claims.claim: Edward Emerson Barnard measured the record motion of Barnard's Star in 1916.
Barnard's Star was captured on astronomical photographic plates as early as 1888 prior to its formal recognition.
Barnard's Star has the fastest proper motion across the night sky of any known star.
Barnard's Star travels across the sky at a proper motion rate of roughly 10.3 arcseconds per year.
Barnard's Star moves across the sky a distance equal to the angular diameter of the Moon every 180 years.
Barnard's Star is a red dwarf star located in the constellation Ophiuchus.
Barnard's Star is located roughly six light-years away from Earth.
Barnard's Star is the second-closest star system to Earth after the Alpha Centauri system.
Barnard's Star has an apparent visual magnitude of roughly 9.5, making it invisible to the unaided human eye.
Barnard's Star has approximately 15% to 16% of the Sun's mass.
Barnard's Star has a radius about 19% to 20% of the Sun's radius, making it only slightly larger in diameter than Jupiter.
In the 1960s, Peter van de Kamp claimed to discover gas giant planets around Barnard's Star, but these claims were disproven in the 1970s.
In 2018, astronomers reported a candidate super-Earth (Barnard's Star b), but subsequent research refuted it as a false positive caused by stellar activity.
Barnard's Star is moving toward our solar system at a radial velocity of roughly 110 kilometers per second.
Barnard's Star will make its closest approach to the Sun in roughly 10,000 years, coming within under four light-years.
Project Daedalus selected Barnard's Star in the 1970s as the target destination for a theoretical uncrewed interstellar spacecraft study.

disputed: Prior planetary claims: Peter van de Kamp claimed gas giants in the 1960s (debunked in the 1970s as telescope instrument artifacts) and a 2018 study claimed a super-Earth (debunked as stellar activity). Scripts should attribute these as historical false alarms.
Exact Stellar Speed Wording: Radial velocity toward us is 110 km/s while total space velocity is ~140 to 143 km/s. Scripts should distinguish motion toward Earth from total velocity in space.

Exact Distance at Closest Approach: S1 states 3.75 light-years around 11,800 CE, whereas S6 states 3.9 light-years in just under 10,000 years. Scripts should state 'under 4 light-years in roughly 10,000 years'.
